title: Transient host heap surge: mitigation log and runbook iteration
body:
Summary:

This is a working incident log for a transient host heap surge that caused sporadic OOMs and degraded request latency in the serving runtime during a high-traffic window. The pattern was distinct from prior persistent KV-cache leaks: memory usage grew quickly on a subset of hosts for ~20–90s, then reclaimed, but in some cases triggered OOM-kills. Impact primarily affected low-latency tails and caused a small fraction of in-flight microbatches to fail with checksum/kv-read errors.

Primary impact:
- ~0.6% of requests experienced elevated p95/p99 latency during the spike window (host-local).
- 4 hosts experienced OOM-kills and were removed from rotation by SRE automation, causing momentary capacity reduction.
- No customer data exposure; failures were transient and retried by client route fallback.

Hypothesis summary (progression):
1) Initial triage: sudden host heap growth correlated with background writeback activity (kvcache flush + microbatch memory amplification).
2) Secondary: a recurring allocation pattern when small prefix cache lookups (high QPS) coincided with a maintenance compaction/eviction job; compaction temporarily increased JS/Go heap fragmentation in the worker process, causing peak RSS.
3) Final working theory: race between async writeback (which constructs ephemeral large buffers for batch-snapshots) and concurrent microbatch KV cache population, where the allocation path bypassed the usual pooling due to a new codepath introduced in PR #3382. Under high concurrency this exhausted host recycler headroom and pushed memory into slow-path allocations -> short-lived heap surge -> kernel OOM.

Timeline (UTC):
- 2024-10-30 22:49:10 — Alert: host-az3-gpu-204 crossed mem.usage > 85% (pager fired).
- 2024-10-30 22:49:18 — SRE oncall (Aisha) acknowledged. Initial handoff from automated page notes "ephemeral surge".
- 2024-10-30 22:49:24 — Observed p99 token latency spike for model-route /v1/completions on host group.
- 2024-10-30 22:49:40 — Two more hosts report RSS > 90%.
- 2024-10-30 22:50:05 — Host OOM event: host-az3-gpu-206 OOM-kill serving_runtime_worker. Eviction automation cordoned host.
- 2024-10-30 22:51:00 — Mitigation: scale-up + route-fallback to regional standby.
- 2024-10-30 22:52:30 — SRE triggers soft-restart of serving runtime on affected hosts (graceful drain + restart).
- 2024-10-30 22:55:10 — Memory reclaimed, latency normalized.
- 2024-10-30 23:40:00 — Follow-up stress-run with local synthetic traffic reproduced a smaller spike; engineering engaged.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident: (these should be codified into runbook steps below)
- Enable route-level fallback to smaller quantized model for burst traffic (short term).
- Temporarily reduce background compaction frequency on az3 pool.
- Turn off new pooling bypass introduced in PR #3382 (hotfix revert).
- Increase heap-pressure threshold for automated cordon from 95% -> 92% to trigger earlier eviction.

Evidence and queries used for triage:
- PromQL: 1) host_mem_rss_bytes / host_mem_total_bytes > 0.85 over 10s window to detect spikes.
  - query: avg_over_time(host_process_resident_memory_bytes{job="serving-runtime"}[30s]) / on(instance) host_memory_total_bytes > 0.85
- PromQL: identify hosts doing heavy writeback allocations by tracking 'serving_runtime_buffer_alloc_bytes_total' (custom metric).
  - query: increase(serving_runtime_buffer_alloc_bytes_total[1m]) by (instance)
- Logs: Loki query for writeback stackframes: {|json|} level=error OR level=warn |
  - {app="serving-runtime", component="kv-writeback"} |= "alloc" |= "batch-snapshot"
- Heap profiles: captured pprof snapshots at 22:50:50 from affected hosts (pprof/heap 10s).

Investigation notes:
- pprof diff shows a spike in allocations attributed to bytes.Buffer growth paths in new batch-snapshot path (file: writeback/batch.go).
- The new codepath bypassed the shared buffer pool when snapshot size > X (fallback condition), causing transient per-request large allocations under certain concurrency interleavings.
- Replica GC timing: hosts with the most frequent microbatch start/stop cycles showed higher fragmentation. The kernel OOM was triggered when several large transient buffers were live concurrently (peak ~1.8× baseline).
- Reproduced locally by running 2000 concurrent microbatched requests + background compaction job every 2s.

Actionable short-term runbook (operational steps for new oncall):
1) Acknowledge and confirm pager scope.
2) Identify impacted host pool: PromQL query for mem > 85% across serving-runtime job (see above).
3) If > 2 hosts impacted in pool: scale regional standby pool by +20% and enable route-fallback for at-risk routes.
4) For each host with RSS > 92% and rising: cordon host (k8s) and initiate graceful drain: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120
5) If OOM already occurred: collect pprof snapshots from /debug/pprof/heap (10s, 2x), copy logs, and create JIRA-INC ticket with attachments.
6) If more than 1 OOM in same AZ within 15 minutes: disable writeback compaction via feature flag: ff/kv_writeback_compaction = false (ops-console).
7) Apply hotfix if available: revert PR #3382 (hotfix revert PR link in linked artifacts), or set env var SERVING_BUFFER_POOL_BYPASS=false and restart service process.
8) After restart, verify mem stabilizes for 10 minutes before uncordoning.
9) Post-incident: run a 30m synthetic traffic soak with compaction schedule restored at a lower frequency, capture pprof every 60s.

Recommended mid-term engineering actions:
- Buffer-pooling: ensure all large allocation paths use the segmented pool; add strong unit + integration tests that assert pool hits under high concurrency.
- Backpressure: add admission control when background compaction starts if concurrent live microbatches > N.
- Compaction scheduling: avoid global compaction at peak traffic windows — make it shard-aware and stagger across hosts.
- Observability: add a derived metric 'transient_allocation_burst_count' and an alert for > 10 bursts per minute.
- Chaos tests: add an automated test that runs compaction while high-QPS microbatch traffic is active to catch regressions pre-merge.

Follow-ups and owners: (owners will take these into next sprint)
- Engineering (serving-runtime): Mateo Ruiz — PR to rework pool bypass and add tests (JIRA-ENG-1259).
- Product infra: Jun Park — change compaction schedule defaults, add shard-aware compaction.
- Observability: Renée Dubois — add derived metrics and dashboard tile for transient allocation bursts.
- SRE process: Aisha Patel — update runbook (this doc) and lower cordon threshold; update automated cordon config.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How many other PRs touch the buffer path? Search codeowners and run a targeted audit.
- Can we make compaction adapt to per-host live microbatch counts rather than global time?
- What is the customer-visible SLA impact threshold for triggering on-call instead of auto-fallback?

Appendix: useful commands and references
- pprof heap snapshot: curl -sS http://<host>:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap1.pb && go tool pprof -http=:8081 heap1.pb
- collect logs for a host: gcloud compute ssh <host> -- sudo journalctl -u serving-runtime -o short-iso --since "2024-10-30 22:40:00" > /tmp/serving-runtime-logs.txt
- temporary feature flag toggle (ops-console): https://ops-console/flags/kv_writeback_compaction (search ff id = kv_writeback_compaction)

Notes to self (informal):
- The spike felt like a "burst" more than a leak — ephemeral but high amplitude. Keep language precise in postmortem: "transient allocation surge due to pooling bypass" instead of using 'leak'.
- Reproduced locally after turning down GC pacing + raising concurrency: good reproduction criteria documented in linked artifact.

Attachments: pprof snapshots (attached to JIRA-INC-4821), log excerpts, reproducer script (repro/heap-surge-repro.sh)

Status: in_review — will convert to final runbook after engineering patch lands and we've validated in staging with longer soak.

End of document.
